method: Preliminary individual screening; source locators compared in accessible modern translations and reference pages, without complete Hebrew critical-edition collation. All candidates unpublished. Earlier PRs and live private queue require reconciliation.

verses.finding: Divorced women receive fair provision; no precise earlier textual counterpart established.
Concluding exhortation to understand divine signs; no source-specific earlier parallel assigned.
People fleeing death and divine restoration; possible resurrection motifs, but no particular earlier narrative securely identified.
Exhortation to fight in God's way; no precise earlier passage assigned.
Metaphor of a good loan to God and multiplied recompense; no text-specific parallel established in this pass.
Israelites request a king from a prophet after Moses; 1 Samuel 8:4–22 offers a clear earlier royal-request narrative, with different framing.
Talut chosen as king despite objection over wealth; 1 Samuel 9–10 recounts Saul's selection, with different objections and signs.
Ark as sign of kingship, borne by angels; 1 Samuel 4–6 discusses the ark but does not present this same installation sign.
Talut tests troops with river water; Judges 7:4–7 presents Gideon's water selection, but the leader, test mechanics, and narrative placement differ.
Prayer for patience and victory before facing Jalut; related battle context in 1 Samuel 17, but no identical prayer established.

candidates.shared: Israelite elders ask a prophet for a king to lead them in war.
candidates.difference: Samuel objects to monarchy as rejection of divine kingship; Qur'an emphasizes a prior refusal to fight after asking.

candidates.shared: Saul/Talut selected for kingship amid human reservations.
candidates.difference: Qur'an stresses knowledge and physique over wealth; Samuel gives a different selection and recognition narrative.

candidates.shared: Troops are separated using their behavior at water before a battle.
candidates.difference: Biblical leader is Gideon, not Saul; criteria and purpose differ, so this cannot be treated as the same historical event.
